name: Haile Selassie
info: Haile Selassie I, born Tafari Makonnen, was Emperor of Ethiopia from 1930 to 1974, remembered for his appeal to the League of Nations against the Italian invasion, his reforms, and his place in Rastafari.

facts.born: 23 July 1892, in the village of Ejersa Goro, Hararghe province, Ethiopia; son of Ras Makonnen Wolde Mikael, of the Solomonic dynasty
facts.died: 27 August 1975, Addis Ababa, while held under house arrest; killed on the orders of the Derg regime, which reported a death from respiratory failure
facts.role: Regent Plenipotentiary and Crown Prince of Ethiopia (1916–1930); Negus (1928–1930); Emperor of Ethiopia (1930–1974); first chairman of the Organisation of African Unity (1963)
facts.known: Ethiopia's first written constitution (1931); his address to the League of Nations in 1936; exile in Bath and return to Addis Ababa in 1941; confirming the abolition of slavery in 1942; presiding over the founding of the Organisation of African Unity; his overthrow by the Derg in 1974; his divine importance in Rastafari

t: As regent from 1916 and emperor from 1930, Haile Selassie pursued a cautious modernisation of Ethiopia, with a written constitution in 1931 and a revised one in 1955, against the steady resistance of the landed nobility.

Driven into exile by the Italian invasion of 1935–1936, he pleaded Ethiopia's case before the League of Nations, returned to Addis Ababa in 1941, and later presided over the founding of the Organisation of African Unity.
His government has been criticised as autocratic, famine and unrest eroded its support, and in 1974 the Derg deposed him; he was killed in its custody in 1975.
dyk: On his 1924 tour of Europe Ras Tafari travelled with a pride of lions, which he gave as gifts to the president and prime minister of France and to King George V. In return for two lions the United Kingdom handed back the imperial crown of Emperor Tewodros II, taken in 1868.
ev: Tafari Makonnen is born on 23 July in the village of Ejersa Goro, in the Hararghe province of Ethiopia
After Lij Iyasu is deposed on 27 September, Tafari is proclaimed Crown Prince and Regent Plenipotentiary under Empress Zewditu
Following the death of Empress Zewditu he is crowned emperor on 2 November at the Cathedral of St. George in Addis Ababa, taking the regnal name Haile Selassie I
He introduces Ethiopia's first written constitution on 16 July, providing for a bicameral legislature
Defeated at the Battle of Maychew, he leaves Ethiopia on 2 May and addresses the League of Nations on the Italian invasion
He enters Addis Ababa on 5 May, exactly five years after the Italian forces had entered the city
He presides over the formation of the Organisation of African Unity and is elected its first chairperson
The Derg, a committee of junior officers and enlisted men, deposes the 82-year-old emperor on 12 September

sections.early:
Haile Selassie was born Tafari Makonnen on 23 July 1892 in the village of Ejersa Goro, in the Hararghe province of Ethiopia. As a child he was known as Lij Tafari Makonnen; the name Haile Selassie, "Power of the Trinity" in Ge'ez, was given to him at his infant baptism. His father, Ras Makonnen Wolde Mikael, was a grandson of King Sahle Selassie of Shewa and a general of the First Italo–Ethiopian War who played a key role at the Battle of Adwa. His mother, Woizero Yeshimebet Ali Abba Jifar, was the daughter of a ruling chief from Were Ilu in Wollo province. Through his paternal grandmother, an aunt of Emperor Menelik II, he belonged to the Solomonic dynasty, whose tradition traces every monarch to Menelik I, described in the Kebra Nagast as the son of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba.

Ras Makonnen arranged for Tafari and his first cousin Imru Haile Selassie to be taught in Harar by Abba Samuel Wolde Kahin, an Ethiopian Capuchin friar, and by Dr. Vitalien, a surgeon from Guadeloupe. On 1 November 1905, at the age of 13, Tafari was named Dejazmach, a title roughly equivalent to count. His father died at Kulibi in 1906. Tafari assumed the titular governorship of Selale in 1906, was appointed governor over part of Sidamo in 1907, and was made governor of Harar in 1910 or 1911. It is alleged that in his late teens he was married to Woizero Altayech and that his daughter Princess Romanework was born of this union. On 3 August 1911 he married Menen Asfaw of Ambassel, niece of the heir to the throne, Lij Iyasu; the marriage lasted 50 years.
sections.rise:
Lij Iyasu, the designated but uncrowned emperor from 1913, offended the nobles of the court, and his flirtation with Islam was considered treasonous by the Ethiopian Orthodox leadership. On 27 September 1916 he was deposed on the grounds of conversion to Islam; how far Tafari contributed to the movement has been much discussed. Menelik II's daughter was named Empress Zewditu, and Tafari, who drew support from both progressive and conservative factions, became Ras, Crown Prince and Regent Plenipotentiary. On 27 October an army loyal to them defeated and captured Iyasu's father, Negus Mikael of Wollo, at the Battle of Segale. Tafari's position was weak at first, but Zewditu's authority gradually declined while his grew.

As regent he continued the cautious modernisation begun by Menelik II. He secured Ethiopia's admission to the League of Nations in 1923 by promising to eradicate slavery, and in 1924 toured Europe and the Middle East. In 1928 Dejazmach Balcha Safo, governor of Sidamo, came to Addis Ababa with a large army; Tafari had the army bought off and replaced him. After a failed palace coup that September, the Empress crowned Tafari Negus, or king, on 7 October 1928. Conservatives saw two monarchs in one capital as an insult to the crown, and her husband, Ras Gugsa Welle, marched from Gondar; he was defeated and killed at the Battle of Anchem on 31 March 1930. Zewditu died on 2 April 1930, of paratyphoid fever and complications from diabetes, and Tafari was crowned emperor as Haile Selassie I on 2 November 1930.
sections.deeds:
On 16 July 1931 Haile Selassie introduced Ethiopia's first written constitution, which provided for a bicameral legislature, kept power with the nobility and limited the succession to his own descendants. Italy invaded in early October 1935, with a modern army, a large air force and chemical weapons. After the northern armies were destroyed he led the last of them at the Battle of Maychew on 31 March 1936 and was defeated. His council agreed that he should leave to put Ethiopia's case to the League of Nations at Geneva; he departed on 2 May 1936 and told the assembly that Italy was using chemical weapons on military and civilian targets alike. The League agreed only to partial sanctions. He spent the years 1936 to 1941 at Fairfield House in Bath, England.

On 18 January 1941 he crossed from Sudan into Ethiopia, and on 5 May 1941 he entered Addis Ababa, urging his people not to return the atrocities they had suffered. On 27 August 1942 he confirmed the legal basis for the abolition of slavery, with severe penalties for slave trading. Ethiopia became a charter member of the United Nations, and in 1950 the General Assembly federated Eritrea with it. Between 1941 and 1959 he worked for the autocephaly of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, granted in 1959. A revised constitution of 1955 made the lower house of parliament an elected body while he retained effective power. In 1963 he presided over the formation of the Organisation of African Unity, with its headquarters in Addis Ababa, and was elected its first chairperson.
sections.opponents:
The landed aristocracy consistently opposed his changes. A progressive tax scheme of 1942 failed against the nobility, and where new land taxes were imposed landowners often passed the burden on to the peasants. A single progressive income tax in 1966 provoked a revolt in Gojjam, which was repressed, though enforcement of the tax was abandoned. His decision to leave Ethiopia in 1936 was itself contested: the nobleman Blatta Tekle Wolde Hawariat objected strenuously to a monarch fleeing before an invader. On 13 December 1960, while he was in Brazil, the imperial guard staged a coup and proclaimed his elder son, Asfa Wossen, emperor; the army and police crushed it, but it had support among students and the educated classes.

Critics have called his administration autocratic and illiberal, and the 1955 constitution has been criticised for reasserting "the indisputable power of the monarch". In 1948 a rebellion of Harari and Somali Muslims in Harar was met with a violent crackdown, and many Hararis left; the historians Tim Carmichael and Roman Loimeier hold that he was directly involved in its suppression. According to some sources the Oromo language was de facto banned from education and administration late in his reign. A famine in Tigray from 1958 is estimated to have killed approximately 100,000 people. Eritrea's federation was dissolved and the territory made a province in 1962, and the Imperial Army committed atrocities in the war against Eritrean separatists. In his last years Freedom House rated Ethiopia "Not Free", and dissidents were imprisoned and tortured.
sections.last:
By the 1970s student unrest was a regular feature of Ethiopian life, and conservatives at court, in parliament and in the church blocked his proposals for land reform. Famine, mostly in Wollo, is estimated to have killed 40,000 to 80,000 Ethiopians between 1972 and 1974; some reports suggest that the Emperor was unaware of its extent, while others assert that he knew of it. In February 1974 four days of riots in Addis Ababa over inflation left five dead. The army mutinied, beginning in Asmara, the prime minister, Aklilu Habte-Wold, resigned on 27 February, and a four-day general strike followed in March.

The Derg, a group of junior officers and enlisted men set up in June to investigate the military's demands, deposed the 82-year-old emperor on 12 September 1974. He was held briefly at the 4th Army Division and then under house arrest in the palace. On 23 November 60 former high officials, among them his grandson Rear Admiral Iskinder Desta, were executed by firing squad, and the Derg announced the end of the Solomonic dynasty. State media reported that he had died on 27 August 1975 of respiratory failure after a prostate operation, an account that Asrat Woldeyes rejected. In 1994, three years after the Derg fell, an Ethiopian court found former officers guilty of strangling him in his bed on the regime's orders. His bones had been found under a concrete slab on the palace grounds in 1992, and on 5 November 2000 he was given a funeral at the Holy Trinity Cathedral in Addis Ababa, which the government declined to make an official imperial one.
sections.legacy:
Haile Selassie is widely considered a defining figure in modern Ethiopian history, and his legacy remains a topic of debate. He played a leading role in founding Addis Ababa University and the Organisation of African Unity, the precursor of the African Union. His 1936 speech made him an icon for anti-fascists around the world, and he is remembered as a prominent anti-colonial leader. In the 1950s he was widely regarded as a modernising and capable ruler; in the 1970s famine and economic turmoil damaged that reputation. The Derg accused him of hoarding millions in Swiss banks, and Ethiopian media in 1974 claimed a fortune of 11 billion dollars, though records put his net worth at £22,000 as late as 1959. In recent years there has been a resurgence of nostalgia for his reign and of support for constitutional monarchy.

In Rastafari, a religion that emerged in Jamaica in the 1930s after news of his coronation arrived there, he is accorded divine importance; among adherents he is called the returned Jesus and the messiah who will lead the peoples of Africa and its diaspora to freedom. He was himself an adherent of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. When he visited Jamaica on 21 April 1966, approximately one hundred thousand Rastafari met him at the airport, a day commemorated as Grounation Day. In a 1967 interview he denied his alleged divinity, though many Rastafari do not read it as a denial. Most Rastafari rejected the funeral of 2000 and did not accept that the bones were his.

summary: Haile Selassie I ruled Ethiopia as regent from 1916 and as emperor from 1930 to 1974. He resisted the Italian invasion, pleaded his country's case before the League of Nations, returned from exile in 1941 and helped found the Organisation of African Unity. Deposed by the Derg in 1974 and killed in its custody in 1975, he is held to be divine by Rastafari.

notes: The article dates the League of Nations address to 12 May 1936 in one paragraph and speaks of 'his June 1936 speech' in the next (the external link also says June 1936). I gave only the year in the event and no day in the text.
Place of death: the lead says the Jubilee Palace in Addis Ababa; the body says he was moved 'back to the Grand Palace' for his house arrest. I wrote 'the palace' / 'Addis Ababa'.
The article says Time named him Man of the Year 'for 1935' at the beginning of 1936, and later 'In 1935 ... he was even named'. Left out.

The article has a contradictory passage: imprisonment and torture of political dissidents, yet 'no more than ten political prisoners during his entire reign'. I kept the first (with the Freedom House rating) and left the second out.
The article spells the historian 'Tim Carmicheal'; I wrote 'Carmichael' - editor to decide whether to keep the article's spelling.

Eritrea: the article says a UN resolution of 2 December 1950 federated Eritrea with Ethiopia; that 'Eritrea's elected parliament voted to become the fourteenth province of Ethiopia in 1962'; and that the federation was dissolved and the parliament shut down. The lead says he 'dissolved the Federation ... and annexed Eritrea'. I wrote 'the federation was dissolved and the territory made a province in 1962'.
Tigray famine: the article says it was 'already two years old' in summer 1958 and ended in August 1961; I wrote 'from 1958', following the heading '1958 famine of Tigray'.
Human Rights Watch is named in the lead as one group that has called the administration autocratic and illiberal; I wrote 'Critics have called' to save room - could be named.
The 1936 exile: 'His council agreed' stands for 'a stormy session of the council of state' and further debate; the decision was not unanimous (given in the opponents section).
The mother's descent (paternally Oromo, maternally Silte) and the father's disputed paternal lineage were left out for length.
Left out for length (all in the article): the Bale revolt from 1963, the Kagnew Battalion in Korea and troops for the Congo, the Shashamane land grant of 1948, the 2019 memorial at the African Union.

Asrat Woldeyes is named in the article without any description (it says only that he denied that complications had occurred and rejected the government version); the text therefore names him without saying who he was.
